sentences.text: The harbour wall at Kalamáki was finished in 1961 and the turtle was already old, and this is not a family legend — it is in a photograph in the town hall.
The photograph is of the opening.
There are forty or fifty people on the new mole in good clothes and there is a priest and a man from the ministry and a boy on the parapet who is now eighty-two and runs the hardware shop.
And in the bottom right of the frame, in the shallows inside the arm of the wall, there is a shape.
Nobody who has not lived there sees it.

Ela's grandmother had pointed it out to her at about six with a fingernail on the glass, and once you have seen it you cannot see the photograph any other way: the flat oval, the notch out of the back edge of the shell, the head just under.
The notch is the point.

It is a piece missing from the rear margin of the carapace, about the width of two fingers, with a smooth healed edge, and the turtle on the beach at Kalamáki in the summer of 2026 has it in exactly the same place.
Ela is twelve and has been told that this is not proof of anything and that the sea is full of damaged turtles.
She has heard that from four adults and it is perfectly true and she has never believed it for a second, and she has the photograph on her phone at a resolution that the town hall did not authorise.
The argument against her is good and she can make it better than any of the adults who made it to her.
Loggerheads take damage constantly.
They get hit by propellers and caught in gear and bitten, and a healed notch in the rear margin is one of the commonest injuries there is.

On a beach that gets between four and eleven nesting females a year, over sixty years, you would expect a great many notched turtles and there is no reason at all to think that two photographs sixty-five years apart show the same animal.

What Ela has against that is the position of the notch, which is the same to within about a centimetre, and the fact that nobody in Kalamáki has ever, in her lifetime or her grandmother's, reported a second notched turtle.
She is aware that this is not evidence.
She would like it noted that she has never once claimed it was.
A loggerhead can live somewhere in the region of sixty or seventy years and possibly a great deal longer; nobody knows, because nobody has ever followed one all the way through.

If the turtle in the 1961 photograph was breeding then, she was at least twenty-five, which puts her hatching somewhere in the middle 1930s, which means she came out of that sand before the road, before the electricity, before the wall, and before every single person now living in that town.
The town knows this.
It is not a secret and it is not particularly discussed.

She is *i grià* — the old woman — and she comes up the beach for about six nights in July, and everybody leaves her alone, and the tavernas turn their sea-facing lights off in July because they always have.
The light business is worth explaining because visitors find it inconvenient and complain about it in reviews.
Hatchlings come out at night and they go towards the brightest thing on the horizon, which for the whole history of the species has been the sea reflecting the sky.
A lit taverna forty metres inland is brighter, and they go up the beach instead of down it, and they die in the road.
Nobody in Kalamáki has ever needed that explained.

The tavernas were turning their seaward lights off in July before there was a word for it and before there was a law about it, and the law, when it came in 2010, changed nothing whatsoever in that town.
